script.title: Direct Tax vs Indirect Tax
script.caption_hook: The shopkeeper pays GST to the government. So who really pays it?

lines.say: Ma'am, the shopkeeper pays GST to the government. So who really pays the tax?
Good question! Taxes are direct or indirect. The difference is who finally bears the burden.
So who bears it in income tax?
The earner. Direct tax falls on a person's income or wealth, like income tax.
It falls on supply, sale or import of goods and services, like GST. The burden is passed on.
Say you buy a shirt for ₹1,000, with GST at 18%. You pay ₹1,180 in all.
So the shopkeeper isn't bearing it?
Right. He must collect and pay it to government, but the burden passes to you.
So how do I decide in an MCQ?
Ask: can the burden be passed on? No means direct. Yes means indirect.
Even if the seller deposits it?
Yes. Who deposits doesn't matter. Remember: direct is me, indirect is pass on.

check_notes: Checker: Line 8 voice and calc board (also Line 10 flow board): a ₹1,000 shirt does not attract 18% GST. After the GST rate rationalisation effective 22 Sep 2025 (within the June 2026 law basis), readymade garments up to ₹2,500 per piece are taxed at 5%. Even before that, apparel up to ₹1,000 was at 5%. Correct it to: 'Say you buy a shirt for ₹1,000 with GST at 5%. You pay ₹1,050 in all.' Then change the boards to '₹1,000 + ₹50 GST = ₹1,050' and 'Buyer pays ₹1,050; Govt gets ₹50 GST'. Better still, use an item that is clearly taxed at 18%, or present the rate as an assumed figure ('assume GST at 18%') so you don't rely on a rate the item doesn't carry.

Checker: Line 10 voice and flow board: 'He must collect and pay it to government' / 'gets ₹180 via seller' suggests the shopkeeper alone deposits the whole tax. Because of input tax credit, the ₹180 (or ₹50 after the correction) reaches the government in stages across the supply chain, and the retailer deposits only the tax on his value addition. Suggested wording: 'He collects it and, along with the earlier sellers, it reaches the government, but the burden passes to you.' (minor wording)

Checker: Line 4 / Line 6 board 'On income or wealth': wealth tax was abolished from AY 2016-17. As a general definition this is fine, but consider 'income or wealth (e.g., income tax)' so it doesn't suggest wealth tax still applies. (minor)
reviewer_note: GST 18% is stated as an assumption ("say GST at 18%"), so the ₹1,000 + ₹180 = ₹1,180 example is self-contained. Wording says the seller must collect and pay GST (no claim that he deposits the full ₹180 in cash, ITC ignored). Indirect tax is on goods and services; direct is on income or wealth.
